Somewhere in the hills above an enemy camp, someone has already placed the materials needed to start a fire. They placed them weeks ago, when the general saw the season turning dry. Now the general is watching the sky, reading the constellations, waiting for the day when the wind will be right. The fire can only work if the conditions are right. Acting before they are ready means wasting what was prepared — and the enemy learns something in the process.

Chapter 12 begins with a list: five targets for fire attack. Soldiers in camp, stores, baggage trains, arsenals and magazines, and dropping fire directly on the enemy. The targets are not equal. Soldiers can be replaced. Stores take time to rebuild. Arsenals and magazines — the depots that sustain a campaign over months — are the hardest to reconstitute. The list is a ranking of how much the enemy loses and how long they take to recover.

Before fire is used, four conditions must be met. The agent must be in place. The season must be dry. The day must be one when the wind rises. The wind direction must be known. All four — not three, not almost all. If any condition is missing, the answer is to wait, not to improvise. A commander who acts before the conditions are ready does not show initiative; he wastes what was prepared and gives the enemy a warning.

When fire breaks out inside an enemy camp, the general outside must watch first. If chaos follows the fire, strike — coordinate the outside attack with the inside disruption. If no chaos follows, wait. Do not attack simply because fire was set. The moment for striking is defined by what can be seen, not by what was planned.

The chapter closes with something that surprised everyone who first read it. Sun Tzu says: anger may pass. Vexation may pass. But a kingdom destroyed cannot be rebuilt. The dead cannot be restored. Move only when the advantage is certain, when victory can be calculated, when danger can be avoided. Never move from anger alone. The consequences of decisions made in anger outlast the anger that caused them.

The five-target hierarchy — soldiers, stores, baggage, arsenals, dropping fire on the enemy — ranks disruption by reconstitution cost. The highest-leverage targets are the hardest to reconstitute. The hierarchy is a corrective against that preference — but only for a commander who can afford to accept the slower timeline that high-leverage targeting requires.

The four preconditions form a decision gate that is explicit about its standard: all four or defer. The gate is correct as a filter, but incomplete as a framework. It tells the commander what conditions must be met; it does not address how long the commander should wait for them or what to do when the opportunity that the fire attack was designed to exploit is degrading while the conditions are still unmet. The gate has no rule for its own temporal cost.

The response timing doctrine is where precision requires something the doctrine cannot specify: criteria for upheaval. The doctrine says to coordinate the external attack with internal chaos — but it does not define what counts as chaos and what counts as a controlled response that merely looks like chaos. Two observers watching the same enemy camp after a fire will reach different conclusions. The doctrine requires real-time judgment, which requires pre-agreed criteria for the signals that will trigger or defer the external attack. Those criteria must be established before the fire is lit, not decided at the moment they are needed.

Fire is multiplicative; water is additive. But the classification depends on the enemy's actual resource structure, which is an intelligence product. An arsenal that appears to be the substrate is additive if the enemy has equivalent supply elsewhere. The fire/water framework is a diagnostic — it requires inputs about the enemy's reconstitution capacity that may not be available. A commander who treats fire as unconditionally multiplicative without verifying the enemy's substitute resources has selected the right category but may be executing the wrong type of action.

The closing argument is the book's most direct confrontation with emotional motivation. Anger may pass. Vexation may give way to satisfaction. A kingdom destroyed does not come back. The three-condition rule — advantage certain, victory calculable, danger avoidable — is designed to hold at the moment when emotion makes acting feel necessary and evaluation feel redundant. But the rule has a gap: it is evaluated by the same commander who may want to act. A motivated commander will find inputs that support the conclusion he has already reached. The rule stops motivated reasoning in theory. It relies on character to stop it in practice.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Five targets, ranked by reconstitution cost: soldiers (highest replacement speed), stores and baggage (medium), arsenals and magazines (lowest replacement speed, highest strategic disruption durability). The hierarchy encodes a choice: fast tactical effect from targeting soldiers versus slower, more durable operational collapse from attacking the substrate. The chapter implies a preference for the substrate — but the preference requires accepting a longer timeline to visible effect and resisting the pressure to target what produces the fastest result. A commander who systematically prefers immediate effects will underinvest in the targets the hierarchy prioritizes.

Four preconditions: agent in place, season dry, day with rising wind, wind direction known. Any one unmet closes the gate. The framework is correct as a readiness filter, but incomplete as a decision framework: it prescribes deferral when conditions are unmet but provides no rule for when deferral itself becomes wrong. A fire attack that waits for all four conditions may wait long enough that the opportunity it was designed to exploit no longer exists. The framework's silence on the waiting cost is its structural gap — it handles the readiness question but not the question of how long readiness is worth waiting for.

Response timing cannot be pre-calculated. The doctrine says coordinate the external attack with internal upheaval — but upheaval must be defined in advance of the fire being set. Without explicit criteria for what constitutes upheaval (and what constitutes a controlled enemy response that merely appears chaotic), two observers watching the same enemy camp after the same fire will reach different conclusions from the same evidence. Operational precision at the response timing level requires pre-agreed observational criteria, not just the instruction to observe and judge.

Fire is multiplicative: it destroys the substrate of resistance. Water is additive: it reinforces existing force. But the multiplicative classification depends on the enemy's resource structure. Destroying an arsenal that the enemy can replace from an allied source is additive, not multiplicative. The fire/water distinction is a diagnostic category that requires intelligence about substitute resources before it can be applied correctly. A commander who assumes the designated target is the substrate without verifying the enemy's reconstitution capacity may execute fire attack with precision while achieving only additive effect.

The three-condition rule — advantage certain, victory calculable, danger avoidable — is the chapter's governing principle, and it has a self-certification problem. The evaluation is performed by the same commander who may be motivated to act. A commander who is angry will find that advantage appears certain, victory appears calculable, and danger appears avoidable — because he is defining each condition in a way that supports the action he has already decided to take. The rule stops motivated reasoning in form but not in practice. The chapter relies on character — the enlightened ruler who is heedful, the good general who is full of caution — to close a gap that structure cannot close.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Five targets ranked by reconstitution cost: soldiers in camp (immediate tactical effect, rapid personnel replacement), stores (medium-depth logistics), baggage trains (active operational supply), arsenals and magazines (deep substrate, production and transport timescale reconstitution), direct fire on enemy. The hierarchy is a corrective against tactical myopia — the preference for visible, immediate effects over slower, more durable ones. A commander who always targets the fastest effect systematically underinvests in the arsenal-level targets that produce durable operational collapse. The hierarchy requires accepting a longer timeline to visible result in exchange for a result the enemy cannot quickly reverse.

Four preconditions as a necessary gate: agent positioned, season dry, day with rising wind, wind direction known. Any one unmet closes the gate. The framework is designed for deferral as the correct response to partial readiness. Its gap: deferral has a temporal cost the framework does not address. An opportunity that was viable when the conditions were first identified may not be viable by the time all four conditions converge. The framework handles the readiness question but not the question of how long the cost of waiting for full readiness remains below the cost of acting with partial readiness.

Response timing precision requires pre-agreed observational criteria. The doctrine instructs: observe; if upheaval, attack; if no upheaval, wait. But 'upheaval' is a judgment call, and two observers watching the same evidence may judge differently. Operational precision at this level requires explicit definition — before the fire is set — of what counts as the upheaval that triggers attack and what counts as the recovery that defers it. Without those definitions, the observation requirement is a real-time judgment under conditions of stress, which is exactly the environment in which criteria diverge most among observers.

The fire/water distinction requires enemy resource intelligence. Fire is multiplicative if the target is genuinely the substrate of resistance; it is additive if the enemy has substitute resources that reconstitute the substrate after the named target is destroyed. Whether an action is fire or water cannot be determined from the action's description — it requires knowing the enemy's actual resource structure. A command that treats fire attack as unconditionally multiplicative without verifying substitute capacity will execute the right analytical category on false inputs, producing additive effects while expecting multiplicative ones.

The three-condition rule has a structural gap: it is self-certified by the evaluating commander. Advantage certain, victory calculable, danger avoidable — all three require judgment about categories that the motivated commander will define to reach the conclusion he wants. The rule creates the form of evaluation without structural protection against its capture by the very motivation it is designed to check. The chapter closes by naming what fills the gap: character. The enlightened ruler who is heedful. The good general who is full of caution. Structure cannot produce that quality; experience and deliberate cultivation over time can.

point.gentle: **The five fire targets differ not only in strategic leverage but in how long they take to produce visible effect.** Targeting soldiers produces immediate tactical results. Targeting stores and arsenals produces slower but more durable operational collapse. A commander who prefers faster effects will systematically underinvest in the highest-leverage targets.
point.direct: **The target hierarchy encodes a trade-off between tactical speed and strategic durability.** Fast tactical effect from attacking soldiers degrades as the enemy replaces personnel. Durable operational collapse from attacking arsenals compounds as the enemy runs out of what the campaign depends on. Accepting the slower timeline is the strategic choice.
point.competitive: **The hierarchy is a corrective against tactical myopia — the systematic preference for visible, immediate effects over slower, more durable ones.** A commander who always acts on the fastest available result will select soldiers over arsenals and accept a reversible disruption rather than an irreversible operational collapse.

moreDetails.gentle: The sequencing problem has a practical implication: disrupting the supply chain requires time to produce visible effect, and during that time the enemy continues to fight from existing supply. A commander who expects immediate results from targeting arsenals and evaluates success within the first days of the disruption will conclude the attack has failed before the disruption has had time to propagate through the enemy's logistics. The time horizon for evaluating supply-chain disruption must match the time horizon on which supply-chain reconstitution operates — which is typically weeks to months, not days.
moreDetails.direct: The strategic choice between fast tactical and slower operational targeting requires knowing the enemy's reconstitution timeline for each target type. That knowledge is an intelligence product: how quickly can this enemy replace personnel, replenish stores, and reconstitute arsenals? Without that knowledge, the hierarchy is a principle without the inputs needed to apply it to a specific situation. A commander who applies the hierarchy on the assumption that personnel are always faster to replace than materiel may be wrong for a specific enemy with abundant personnel reserves and constrained supply chains.
moreDetails.competitive: The temporal dimension of the five-target hierarchy interacts with the command environment in a specific way: commanders who are evaluated on short-cycle metrics will systematically choose the target with the fastest visible effect, regardless of the hierarchy's strategic preference. The hierarchy is only actionable for a commander whose evaluation horizon matches the time horizon on which the highest-leverage disruption produces its effects. This is the operational constraint on the hierarchy's application: it requires a command structure that supports patient strategic targeting over visible tactical effect.

point.gentle: **The precondition framework creates a waiting cost that the chapter does not resolve.** A commander who waits for all four conditions to converge may wait long enough that the opportunity disappears. The framework prescribes deferral but provides no rule for when deferral itself becomes wrong.
point.direct: **The precondition framework's structural gap is its silence on the temporal cost of waiting.** It handles the readiness question — all conditions met, proceed; any unmet, defer — but not the question of how long the cost of waiting for full readiness remains below the cost of acting with partial readiness. This gap is not resolved elsewhere in the chapter.
point.competitive: **The framework treats the readiness question and the timing question as though they are the same question, but they are not.** A decision gate that produces deferral as the correct answer to incomplete readiness is correct for the readiness question. It is incomplete for the timing question, which asks: at what point does further deferral cost more than the degraded probability of acting before all conditions are met?

moreDetails.gentle: The waiting cost is real in any context where opportunities are time-limited. A fire attack opportunity that was viable when the general began positioning the agent may no longer be viable by the time all four conditions converge — the enemy has moved, the political context has changed, the agent's position has been discovered. The framework's instruction to defer is correct for the readiness question, but the general must also be asking the timing question in parallel, using a different framework that the chapter does not provide. Applying only the precondition framework and ignoring the timing cost produces persistent deferral in an environment where opportunities degrade over time.
moreDetails.direct: The gap between the readiness framework and the timing framework creates a specific failure mode: the commander who correctly follows the precondition framework may find that full readiness arrives at the moment when the opportunity has already passed. The framework has no instruction for this case — it neither acknowledges the timing problem nor provides a rule for resolving the trade-off between partial readiness and a closing window. A complete framework for irreversible high-stakes actions would need both a readiness filter and a timing rule that specifies when partial readiness is preferable to continued waiting.
moreDetails.competitive: The temporal cost of the precondition framework is compounded in competitive environments where the adversary is also preparing. An enemy who has observed the general's preparations may be using the waiting period to counter-prepare — repositioning forces, hardening the targets, relocating the stores. The framework instructs waiting when conditions are incomplete, but the enemy's actions during the waiting period may change the conditions themselves, either by satisfying preconditions the general was missing (changes in weather) or by eliminating the opportunity the general was waiting to exploit (the enemy moves the arsenal). The framework does not address adversarial adaptation during the deferral period.

point.gentle: **Real-time observation of upheaval requires pre-agreed criteria for what counts as upheaval.** Two observers watching the same enemy camp after the same fire will reach different conclusions without explicit definitions established before the fire is lit.
point.direct: **The response timing doctrine requires operational criteria, not just the instruction to observe.** Without pre-defined definitions of upheaval and recovery, observation under stress produces divergent judgments. The precision the doctrine demands cannot be achieved by instruction alone — it requires prior agreement on what the signals mean.
point.competitive: **The observational requirement contains a judgment problem that the doctrine does not resolve.** Upheaval must be distinguishable from a controlled enemy response designed to look like chaos. Without explicit observational criteria agreed before the fire is set, the timing decision defaults to individual judgment under the worst conditions for consistent judgment: high stress, time pressure, and incomplete information.

moreDetails.gentle: The criteria-setting problem is prior to the observation problem. Before deciding what to observe, the general must decide what the observation is looking for — specifically, what level of disorganization, what types of visible breakdown in command, what behavioral signals constitute 'upheaval' rather than 'controlled response under fire.' Setting those criteria in advance transforms the observation into a detection problem — is the criterion satisfied or not — rather than a judgment problem — what does this mean? The criteria-setting step is the one the doctrine assumes but does not prescribe.
moreDetails.direct: The enemy's incentive structure during a fire attack creates an observation problem the doctrine does not address: the enemy may deliberately suppress the appearance of upheaval precisely because they know an external attack is likely if upheaval is observed. A disciplined enemy that contains visible disorganization can defeat the observation requirement by making a disrupted force look like a calm one. The doctrine's instruction to observe and attack when upheaval appears is exploitable by an enemy who understands that the observation is happening. Pre-defined criteria that are harder to fake — quantitative measures of movement, response time, command communication — are more robust to this exploitation than qualitative judgments of apparent chaos.
moreDetails.competitive: The criteria-setting requirement has an organizational implication: for two or more observers to reach consistent conclusions from the same evidence, they must share not just a common instruction but a common operational definition. Building that shared definition requires prior exercise under simulated conditions — not just briefing on the doctrine but practice in applying the criteria to ambiguous cases. A force that has only been briefed on the observe-and-judge requirement, without practicing the criteria application, will produce divergent judgments from observers who all believe they are following the same doctrine.

point.gentle: **Whether fire is multiplicative or additive depends on what the enemy can substitute.** An arsenal destroyed may be multiplicative if the enemy has no other source. It is additive if the enemy can resupply from allies or from a second depot. The distinction requires intelligence about substitute resources.
point.direct: **The additive/multiplicative classification is an intelligence-dependent diagnostic, not a fixed property of the action.** Destroying a target that the enemy can reconstitute from substitute sources produces additive effects — the substrate remains intact through substitution. The classification requires knowing the enemy's full resource structure before it can be applied correctly.
point.competitive: **The fire/water framework is analytically correct but operationally incomplete without enemy resource intelligence.** A command that assumes multiplicative effect from fire attack without verifying the enemy's substitute capacity will execute the right analytical category on false inputs and produce additive results while expecting multiplicative ones.

moreDetails.gentle: The substitute resource problem reveals a general limit on multiplicative thinking: a disruption is only multiplicative to the extent that the target is irreplaceable within the relevant time horizon. If the enemy can reconstitute from a different source within the campaign's relevant time frame, the disruption that appeared multiplicative becomes additive by the time its effects propagate. Knowing whether a target is truly multiplicative requires knowing not just what the target is but what the enemy's alternative sources are — which requires intelligence that may not be available before the attack is committed.
moreDetails.direct: The intelligence requirement for correctly applying the fire/water distinction mirrors the intelligence requirement the chapter 11 ground-type framework identified for correct positional classification. In both cases, the framework is a diagnostic tool whose correct application depends on verified knowledge of the adversary's actual situation. In both cases, the diagnostic applied to false inputs produces confident execution of the wrong type of action. The common structural feature: frameworks that require classification before action are only as reliable as the intelligence that determines the classification.
moreDetails.competitive: The substitute resource problem creates a specific category of intelligence failure: the commander who knows about the primary target but not about the substitute sources will identify the correct target, execute the attack correctly, and reach the wrong strategic conclusion when the disruption fails to produce the expected durable effect. The failure is invisible at the point of target selection and execution — it only becomes visible after the enemy has reconstituted from the substitute. By then, the attack has been consumed and the enemy has been alerted to the vulnerability, making a second attack on the same target type more difficult.

point.gentle: **The three-condition rule cannot guarantee honest evaluation because the same commander who wants to act is the one running the evaluation.** The rule creates the form of discipline without a structural mechanism to ensure the evaluation is not shaped by the conclusion already reached.
point.direct: **The three-condition rule's self-certification problem is its structural gap.** Advantage certain, victory calculable, danger avoidable — all three are evaluative judgments that a motivated commander can define to support an action already decided. The rule stops motivated reasoning in theory. It relies on character to stop it in practice.
point.competitive: **The chapter closes not with a structural solution to the self-certification problem but with a character requirement.** The enlightened ruler who is heedful, the good general who is full of caution — these are dispositional qualities that must be cultivated over time. They are the only guard the chapter provides against a motivated commander who uses the three-condition rule as a rationalization structure rather than an evaluation structure.

moreDetails.gentle: The self-certification problem is most severe precisely when the emotion it is designed to check is strongest. A commander who is mildly annoyed can run the three-condition evaluation with reasonable honesty. A commander who is furious will find that each condition appears satisfied because the anger generates a felt certainty that the action is justified and the evaluation is confirming what he already knows. The rule's value is inversely proportional to the emotional intensity of the state it is designed to govern — it is most necessary when it is least reliable.
moreDetails.direct: A structural guard against self-certification would require a second evaluator who does not share the motivated commander's emotional state and has no stake in the action being taken. The chapter does not prescribe this mechanism, but its closing image — the enlightened ruler who is heedful — implies something like it: a quality of attention to the evaluation process itself that operates independently of the conclusion being evaluated. That quality can be cultivated through practice in non-urgent conditions and applied under pressure, but it cannot be guaranteed by the rule's form alone.
moreDetails.competitive: The self-certification problem interacts with the temporal cost problem from the precondition framework in a specific way. A commander who has been waiting for conditions to converge, watching an opportunity potentially degrade over time, and experiencing increasing frustration with the wait will arrive at the moment of decision in an emotional state that is precisely the one the three-condition rule is designed to check. The frustration of waiting may produce the same distorted evaluation as anger — a strong felt sense that the conditions are now met and action is justified, regardless of whether the inputs to the evaluation have actually changed. The rule must operate at this convergence point, against both the accumulated frustration and the motivated conclusion, with only the commander's character as the mechanism.
